chapter: Ben Pollack band and New York
title: Practice, warming up and breathing from the diaphragm
summary: He explains woodshedding, endurance, and breathing from the diaphragm, with a remark about being yourself.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Lips, teeth and breath: the physical craft of brass playing

blocks.x: Well I suppose that's a slang expression. Would you tell posterity what woodshedding means. (LAUGHTER).

Woodshedding means to take it out in the barn, go out in the barn and practice. Very difficult to practice a cornet because of the tones and things like that. It's your coordination, breathing correct and your lips loose and functioning and warmed up. It takes a little while. As a matter of fact it takes me longer now than it ever did to warm up. But practicing, you must practice. If you don't practice every day you'll never make it. You've got to practice.
Let's see, you loose your lip huh? (LAUGHTER).
Yes, you loose your endurance. You loose the endurance. You must have a lot of endurance.
Did you take breathing exercises as actors do in learning to play that kind of instrument?

Well yes, you have to learn to blow from you diaphragm to begin with. That's where you blow from. And you lock it up down there and release it coordinately with your blowing you know which should become second nature. Becomes subconscious after a while, after you know you're breathing correctly.
I was listening to your phrasing and it's intimately of course involved with your, with breathing. Just as it is with a singer.
Oh yes, and that I think is a beautiful thing about your playing.

It flows through the air. But you do it all subconsciously after you learn how to breathe correctly. Which is breathing, taking it down in your diaphragm. If you practice it, breathing down in your diaphragm instead of the upper part. You do it naturally when you're talking if you'll notice, you'll breathe down to your diaphragm and then release the air when you need it.

A couple of years ago I was giving a lecture for the American Theater Association and I was in Chicago at the Hilton Hotel I think it was. And I had to stop and take a sip of water. And of course, I'm not a theater person. I'm not trained as an actress really. (LAUGHTER). So I picked up the glass of water and I looked at them, I said, I'm not in theater, I don't know how to breathe and drank my water. And they cracked up. (LAUGHTER).

Well that's being yourself. (LAUGHTER). I find that one of the greatest things in life is just be genuine. Just be yourself. And if you can be yourself everyone appreciates that, really. Instead of trying to put on airs about everything. END TPT2 [End of tape 1 [Tape II-3 3/4 ips
